narrative.text: Presents the Introduction (document objectives, target audience, chapter structure in Figure 1, general considerations, and acknowledgments) and opens Chapter 1 on the context of health information systems. It defines health information systems (Section 1.1.2) and outlines the operational and analytical benefits of electronic health information systems (Section 1.1.3), including reduced data entry errors, automated indicator calculation, and geographical disaggregation.

Presents Section 1.1.1 defining eHealth according to WHO and outlining the six core eHealth components established in PAHO's Strategy and Plan of Action on eHealth (2012–2017) as illustrated in Figure 2: electronic medical records, telehealth, mHealth, eLearning, continuing education in ICTs, and standardization and interoperability.

Covers Section 1.1.4 on immunization information systems, Section 1.2 on the seven-stage lifecycle for developing and implementing a health information system, and Section 1.3 on common reasons electronic health information systems fail, before opening Chapter 2 on individualized immunization registries. It defines what an electronic immunization registry (EIR) is (Section 2.1, with a country case study from Uruguay), compares aggregated, paper-based nominal, and electronic nominal registries (Section 2.2), and summarizes the benefits of EIRs for recipients, EPI performance, management, and research (Section 2.3).

Presents Section 2.4.1 (and 2.4.1.1) on the registration of individuals in an EIR, emphasizing exhaustive, early inclusion of the entire target population—ideally at birth via links to civil or live-birth registries, newborn BCG/Hepatitis B vaccination, and migration databases—across public, social security, private, and NGO providers so the EIR can serve as an accurate population denominator.

Presents Section 2.4 summarizing the four core pillars of an ideal EIR in Figure 7 (registration of individuals, registration of vaccination events, reports and individual monitoring, and system characteristics), Figure 8 on multisectoral EIR relationships, a country case study on Peru's child registry, and Section 2.4.1.2 on unique individual identification using national ID numbers, maternal-child links, biometrics, and core demographic variables.

Covers Section 2.4.2 on registering vaccination events (administered biologics, all public/private vaccination events, vaccine lot traceability, and ESAVI monitoring, with a Bogotá SINV case study), Section 2.4.3 on reporting and individual monitoring, Section 2.4.4 on system usability, timeliness, flexibility, and confidentiality, and Section 2.5 on assessing readiness to develop an EIR (Table 1). It also spans Chapter 3 Sections 3.1–3.3.4 on strategic and operational planning, defining system scope across functional, geographical, population, and sector dimensions, and assessing existing information systems, human resources, information flows, and IT infrastructure.

Presents Section 3.3.5 on financial resources for an EIR, outlining key planning questions to evaluate capital and maintenance cost estimates, availability of domestic and external funding across the full system lifecycle, and long-term financial sustainability.

Covers Section 3.3.6 on monitoring EIR implementation against the operational plan and budget, and Section 3.3.7 on forming a multidisciplinary working group and engaging stakeholders across local, intermediate, and national levels, summarized in Table 2.

Covers Section 3.4 on mapping current information flows and redesigning business processes using the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM, Figure 11), Section 3.5 on lifecycle cost categories and investment justification (Table 3), and Section 3.6 on managing the transition from non-individualized systems to an EIR, including historical data entry options (Tables 4 and 5). It also opens Chapter 4 with Section 4.1 on selecting standardized person, residence, and vaccination variables for an EIR.

Covers Sections 4.2 through 4.5 on essential EIR functions across local, intermediate, national, and community levels (Table 7), practical utility and vaccination strategy support (Table 8), technical team roles and responsibilities (Table 9), and measuring system success across implementation stages (Table 10), before opening Chapter 5 (Section 5.1) on evaluating environmental readiness and online, offline, or hybrid connectivity modalities.

Presents Table 12 comparing the advantages, disadvantages, and data management requirements of offline, online, and hybrid EIR implementation modalities, along with Section 5.2 (and 5.2.1) on non-functional requirements for selecting appropriate technology, mobile offline-first synchronization, and database consolidation across health system levels.

Presents Section 5.2.2 on software usability principles (ease of learning, ease of use, flexibility, and sturdiness per ISO 9126) with an example checklist of usability requirements in Table 13, and Section 5.2.3 introducing compatibility and interoperability criteria (Table 14).

Presents Section 5.2.4 on security requirements for EIRs—covering authentication, role-based access control, audit logs, database encryption on mobile devices, and secure data transmission (Table 15)—and introduces Section 5.3 on reviewing external experiences with similar health information systems.

Covers Section 5.2.5 on software maintainability requirements (Table 16), the remainder of Section 5.3 on repositories of public health informatics experiences, Section 5.4 comparing custom development, commercial off-the-shelf, free/open-source, and SaaS procurement models (Figure 13 and Table 17), and Section 5.5 on scoring and evaluating software procurement proposals (Table 18), before introducing Chapter 6 on monitoring and evaluating EIR data quality.

Presents Section 6.1 on data quality assessment methods (such as DQS and DQA) and core quality dimensions (completeness, timeliness, integrity, accuracy, and precision), Section 6.2 on the importance of systematic data quality management across local-to-national consolidation flows, and Section 6.3.1 on describing and evaluating the national EIR system.
Provides the section heading for Section 6.3 ('Evaluation of performance indicators for identification of inconsistencies') and the subheading number for Section 6.3.2 on page 87.

Covers Section 6.3.2 on analyzing the information system across all levels of responsibility and Section 6.3.3 on EIR data analysis, including schedule validation rules, identifying and resolving duplicate person or vaccine records (Figure 14), managing data updates and incomplete records, and conducting quality checks on consolidated subnational and national databases.

Covers Chapter 7 on future challenges for EIR sustainability—spanning eHealth policies (Table 19), ICT infrastructure and utilization (Table 20), and advanced data quality and use (Table 21)—Chapter 8 on ethical obligations regarding individualized immunization data collection, informed consent, confidentiality, and secondary use, the bibliographic references, and Annexes 1 through 8 (lessons from failed systems, country readiness self-assessment, variable lists, Honduras case study, EIR evaluation criteria, duplicated record exercises, vaccine schedule validation parameters, and database quality analysis examples).

Front matter of the 2017 Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) publication 'Electronic Immunization Registry: Practical Considerations for Planning, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation' (ISBN 978-92-75-11953-2), including copyright and citation metadata, the table of contents, list of acronyms, and preface. It highlights the role of nominal electronic immunization registries (EIRs) in tracking individual vaccination histories across the life course, improving coverage and equity, optimizing EPI management, and supporting vaccine safety and effectiveness research.
